meta.title: Classic ML Model Zoo
meta.thesis: Classic ML Model Zoo is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A churn team must choose a baseline model before trying deep learning. By the end, they should be able to build or review model zoo comparison sheet for logistic regression, trees, and ensembles, measure validated lift over a simple baseline, and catch the failure where a complex model wins the demo but is impossible to debug.

mentalMap.oneLineThesis: The classic model zoo is a set of useful biases: lines, splits, margins, neighbors, ensembles, and clusters each fit different data stories.

modules.title: Linear models set the baseline
modules.sub: Start with a weighted sum that is easy to inspect.
modules.summary: Linear and logistic models are strong first baselines for many tabular tasks.
objectives: Explain a linear model as weighted evidence.
Know when linear assumptions help or hurt.
Use a baseline before complex models.

blocks.title: A linear model is a transparent scorecard

spans.text: Problem anchor: a support team wants to predict customer churn from days since last login, ticket count, plan tier, and billing failures. A linear or logistic model treats each feature as weighted evidence. More billing failures may push churn risk up; more recent logins may push it down.

This family is a good baseline because it is fast, explainable, and hard to overfit compared with very flexible models. It struggles when the decision boundary bends sharply or features interact in ways a weighted sum cannot express.

blocks.analogy: A linear model is a checklist where each item has a weight.

spans.text: Score = 0.8*billing_failures + 0.4*ticket_count - 0.6*recent_login + 0.3*enterprise_plan. A customer with two billing failures, three tickets, a recent login, and no enterprise plan gets 0.8*2 + 0.4*3 - 0.6*1 + 0 = 2.2. The exact numbers are learned, but the structure is inspectable.

blocks.title: Linear baseline
blocks.prompt: Why try a linear/logistic model early?

options.text: It can discover arbitrary clusters without labels.
It is fast, interpretable, and gives a baseline for validation comparison.

blocks.explanation: Baselines make later complexity justify itself.

modules.title: Trees split data into readable rules
modules.sub: Decision trees model interactions by asking feature questions.
modules.summary: Tree models capture nonlinear rules but can overfit without constraints.
objectives: Explain a decision tree as recursive splits.
Name why trees are interpretable and unstable.
Compare tree rules to linear weights.

spans.text: A decision tree might first ask whether billing_failures > 0, then whether days_since_login > 14, then whether support_tickets > 2. That makes interactions easy to express: a stale login may matter more when billing also failed.
Trees are readable, handle mixed feature types, and capture nonlinear splits. They can also memorize quirks if grown too deep, so validation depth and pruning matter.

blocks.title: Case study: the readable but brittle tree

spans.text: The churn tree reveals a useful business rule: billing failure plus no login for 30 days is high risk. But an unconstrained tree also creates a leaf for a rare legacy plan with two training examples. Validation error rises, warning that the rare leaf is memorization.

modules.title: Margins and neighbors use geometry
modules.sub: SVMs and k-nearest neighbors reason from distances and boundaries.
modules.summary: Geometry-based models care about scaling, distance, and support points.
objectives: Explain SVM margins and nearest-neighbor voting in beginner terms.
Choose these models for the right data shape.

blocks.title: Some models look at the map of points

spans.text: A support-vector machine tries to find a boundary with a wide margin between classes. k-nearest neighbors keeps the training examples and predicts by nearby examples. Both depend heavily on feature scale and distance meaning. If account_value ranges to millions while ticket_count ranges to ten, distance becomes distorted unless features are scaled.

modules.title: Code a small zoo comparison
modules.sub: Validation evidence should choose the family, not the name.
modules.summary: A runnable scikit-learn comparison shows baseline, tree, and neighbor tradeoffs.
objectives: Predict which family may overfit with high train score.

blocks.title: Compare three classic classifiers on one split
blocks.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=7, stratify=y)

models = {
    "logistic": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
    "tree_depth_3": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=7),
    "knn_5": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5)),
}

for name, model in models.items():
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    print(name, round(model.score(X_val, y_val), 3))

spans.text: The same split and metric make the comparison fair enough for a first pass. More serious work would add cross-validation, leakage checks, calibration, and slice metrics.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict why logistic and kNN are wrapped in StandardScaler but the tree is not.
predictThenReveal.answer: Logistic regression and kNN are sensitive to feature scale. Trees split by thresholds and usually do not need feature scaling in the same way.

spans.text: Checklist: every model uses the same split; preprocessing is inside a pipeline; distance-based models are scaled; random seeds are fixed for examples; validation, not training score, chooses the candidate; and the report mentions interpretability and prediction cost.

modules.title: Choose by data shape, constraints, and failure cost
modules.sub: The zoo is a decision tool, not a popularity ranking.
modules.summary: Model choice balances validation performance, interpretability, data size, latency, and maintenance.
objectives: Use a decision matrix for model-family choice.
Include clustering as unsupervised exploration, not a supervised substitute.
Write a next-step plan after the first comparison.

blocks.title: Every family carries a bias and an operating cost

spans.text: Linear models are inspectable baselines. Trees express rules but can overfit. SVMs and neighbors need meaningful geometry. Ensembles often improve accuracy but reduce simplicity. Clustering is useful for exploring unlabeled groups, but it does not replace supervised labels for a churn target.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Choose the simplest family that meets validation, interpretability, and deployment constraints.
blocks.useWhen: Use the zoo when beginning a tabular or small-to-medium ML problem and you need a defensible first shortlist.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid treating model families as a leaderboard; the right choice depends on data shape, metric, failure cost, and maintenance.

blocks.title: Zoo decision
blocks.prompt: A linear model and random forest have nearly equal validation performance, but compliance needs explanations. What is the safer first choice?

options.text: The random forest because it is always more advanced.
The linear model, unless the forest adds enough value to justify lower transparency.

blocks.explanation: Operational constraints are part of model selection.

capstone.prompt: For a customer-churn table, compare logistic regression, decision tree, k-nearest neighbors, and random forest. Write what each model assumes, run a small validation comparison, and choose the simplest model that meets the metric and interpretability need. Next rung: add calibration and feature leakage checks.
